specStatements.text: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols.
Students should be able to draw and interpret circuit diagrams.
For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.
Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge. Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation:
charge flow = current × time
[Q = I t]
charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
time, t, in seconds, s
A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.

The current (I) through a component depends on both the resistance (R) of the component and the potential difference (V) across the component. The greater the resistance of the component the smaller the current for a given potential difference (pd) across the component.
Questions will be set using the term potential difference. Students will gain credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage.
Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation:
potential difference = current × resistance
[V = I R]
potential difference, V, in volts, V
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
resistance, R, in ohms, Ω
Required practical activity 3:
Use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. This should include:
• the length of a wire at constant temperature
• combinations of resistors in series and parallel.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
Students should be able to explain that, for some resistors, the value of R remains constant but that in others it can change as the current changes.

The current through an ohmic conductor (at a constant temperature) is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor. This means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes.
The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component.
The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases.
The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.
The applications of thermistors in circuits eg a thermostat is required.
The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.
The application of LDRs in circuits eg switching lights on when it gets dark is required.
Students should be able to:
• explain the design and use of a circuit to measure the resistance of a component by measuring the current through, and potential difference across, the component
• draw an appropriate circuit diagram using correct circuit symbols.
Students should be able to use graphs to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear and relate the curves produced to the ir function and properties.

Required practical activity 4: use circuit diagrams to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: Questions will be set using the term potential difference. Students will gain credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every stem, definition and correct answer in this material uses the term potential difference (abbreviated pd, as the specification itself abbreviates it) rather than voltage. The word voltage is never used to set a question, so a student who has only ever met potential difference is never disadvantaged. Where students' own answers are discussed, it is stated that voltage is an acceptable alternative and earns credit, so nobody is taught that voltage is wrong. The unit is always given as volts, V, and the symbol for the quantity as V, exactly as the specification lists them.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 6 and 7.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Required practical activity 3 is treated purely as a practical skills requirement, and the skills exercised are kept to those the specification names for it: making and recording measurements accurately (lengths of wire, meter readings), safe use of apparatus, and the use of circuit components and meters to measure current, potential difference and resistance. No additional apparatus techniques from other AT statements are introduced or assessed here, and the numbered AT descriptors themselves are not reproduced or examined as recall - they describe what the student does in the laboratory, not content to be learned.

The WS and MS statements themselves are not reproduced, taught or examined here, because they belong to their own section of the specification.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Required practical activity 4 is presented as the construction and use of circuits to obtain I-V characteristics, exercising only the apparatus skills the specification names for it: safe use of apparatus and the use of circuit components, ammeters and voltmeters to measure electrical quantities. Note that this practical lists AT 6 and 7 only, one fewer than Required practical activity 3, and no measurement technique from outside those skills is required of the student here. concepts.definition: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols, so that any physicist can read any circuit diagram. The symbols required are: switch (open and closed), cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor and LDR. A cell is one long thin line and one short thick line; a battery is two or more cells joined in line. A resistor is a plain rectangle; a variable resistor is that rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it. An ammeter is a circle containing A, a voltmeter a circle containing V.

A circuit diagram is drawn with straight lines for the wires and the correct standard symbol for every component. Components in a single closed loop are in series; components on separate branches are in parallel. An ammeter is always drawn in series with the component whose current is being measured, and a voltmeter is always drawn in parallel with (across) the component whose potential difference is being measured. Interpreting a diagram means reading from it which components share a loop, where the source of potential difference is, and what each meter would read.

For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference, such as a cell or a battery. Two conditions are needed together: the circuit must be closed (a complete loop, with any switch closed), and it must contain a source of potential difference. A complete loop of wire with no cell in it carries no current, and a cell connected into a broken circuit drives no charge.

Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge - how much charge passes a point each second. A current of 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point every second. Current is not a flow of energy and it is not the speed of the charges; it is the rate at which charge passes.

Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation charge flow = current × time, written in symbols as Q = I t. This is one of the equations students must be able to recall and apply. Q is the charge flow in coulombs, C; I is the current in amperes, A; t is the time in seconds, s. Time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before the equation is used. Rearranged, I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I.

The coulomb, symbol C, is the unit of charge flow. In the equation Q = I t, charge flow Q is in coulombs, C. One coulomb is the charge that passes a point when a current of one ampere flows for one second. Charge flow is a quantity of charge; it is not a rate, which is why it has a different unit from current.

The ampere, symbol A, is the unit of current; amp is acceptable for ampere. In both Q = I t and V = I R the current I is in amperes, A. One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second, which is why current is described as the rate of flow of charge. Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series.

concepts.term: Current in a single closed loop
concepts.definition: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop. Charge is not used up as it goes round: every coulomb that leaves the cell returns to it. So in a series circuit an ammeter placed anywhere in the loop - before the first component, between two components, or after the last - gives the same reading. What is used up in a component is energy, not charge.

The current (I) through a component depends on both the resistance (R) of the component and the potential difference (V) across the component. The greater the resistance of the component the smaller the current for a given potential difference across the component. Resistance therefore opposes the flow of charge: for a fixed pd, doubling the resistance halves the current.

Potential difference is the quantity that drives charge round a circuit; its symbol is V and its unit is the volt, V. It is measured with a voltmeter connected in parallel with (across) the component. Questions are set using the term potential difference, but a student gains credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage. Potential difference is measured across a component, never through it.

Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation potential difference = current × resistance, written in symbols as V = I R. This is an equation students must be able to recall and apply. Rearranged it gives I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I, so a component's resistance is found by dividing the pd across it by the current through it.

The ohm, symbol Ω, is the unit of resistance. In the equation V = I R, resistance R is in ohms, Ω, when the potential difference V is in volts, V, and the current I is in amperes, A. A component has a resistance of one ohm when a potential difference of one volt across it drives a current of one ampere through it.

Use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. Two factors are investigated: the length of a wire at constant temperature, and combinations of resistors in series and parallel. In each case the pd across the test section is measured with a voltmeter connected across it and the current through it with an ammeter in series, and the resistance is calculated from R = V ÷ I.

For a wire at constant temperature, resistance increases as the length of wire increases; doubling the length doubles the resistance. To keep the temperature constant the circuit is switched on only briefly for each reading, because a current warms the wire and warming a wire changes its resistance. The lengths are measured with a metre rule and the wire is kept straight along it.

concepts.term: Resistors in series and in parallel
concepts.definition: Adding resistors in series increases the total resistance, because the charge must pass through each resistor in turn; the individual resistances are added. Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance, because the charge now has more than one path to flow along; the total is less than the resistance of the smallest single resistor. Both combinations are built and tested in Required practical activity 3.

The current through an ohmic conductor (at a constant temperature) is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor. This means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. Its I-V graph is therefore a straight line through the origin, and the resistance is found from V ÷ I at any point on it, not from the gradient. For some resistors the value of R remains constant in this way, but in other components it can change as the current changes.

The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component. Their I-V graphs are curved rather than straight, so no single value of R describes them, and the resistance must be worked out from V ÷ I at the particular current being used.

The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases. A larger current heats the filament more, so the resistance rises and the I-V graph curves, becoming less steep as the current grows. A filament lamp is therefore not an ohmic conductor, even though its graph does pass through the origin.

The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so effectively no current passes when it is connected the wrong way round. Its I-V graph shows almost no current in the reverse direction and a curve rising steeply in the forward direction once the pd is large enough.

A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance depends on temperature: the resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases. This is the opposite of a metal wire such as a lamp filament, whose resistance rises when it gets hotter. In a circuit at a fixed potential difference, warming a thermistor therefore increases the current through it.

Because a thermistor's resistance changes with temperature, it is used as a temperature sensor in control circuits - for example in a thermostat. When the room cools, the thermistor's resistance rises; when the room warms, the resistance falls. The control circuit detects this change and switches the heater on or off, holding the temperature near a set value. The same idea is used in fire alarms and in oven and fridge controls.
An LDR is a resistor whose resistance depends on light: the resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light its resistance is low; in darkness its resistance is high.

Because an LDR's resistance changes with light intensity, it is used as a light sensor in control circuits - for example switching lights on when it gets dark. As night falls the LDR's resistance rises, the control circuit detects the change and the street lamp is switched on; at dawn the resistance falls again and the lamp is switched off. The same idea is used in burglar alarms and in automatic camera and phone screen brightness controls.

To measure the resistance of a component, connect it in series with a cell, a switch, an ammeter and a variable resistor, and connect a voltmeter in parallel with the component. The ammeter measures the current through the component and the voltmeter the potential difference across it; the resistance is then R = V ÷ I. The variable resistor is adjusted to change the current so that several pairs of readings can be taken, and the correct circuit symbols are used when the diagram is drawn.

A circuit element is linear if its I-V graph is a straight line, which means the current is directly proportional to the potential difference and the resistance is constant. It is non-linear if the graph is a curve, which means the resistance changes. The shape of the curve tells you how: a graph that becomes less steep as the current rises shows resistance increasing, as in a filament lamp, and a graph that becomes steeper shows resistance falling.

Use circuit diagrams to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I-V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature. For each element the pd is varied, pairs of current and pd readings are taken and I is plotted against V. The reverse characteristic of the diode is obtained by reversing the diode's connections in the circuit, and a resistor is included in series with the diode to protect it from a large current.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are in series with a cell. Is the current smaller after the first lamp?
misconceptions.correct: No. A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so the reading is the same before, between and after the lamps.
misconceptions.misconception: The current gets used up as it goes round, so there is less current left after each lamp.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the lamps glowing and know something is being used up, and the everyday word 'current' suggests a supply that runs out. The energy transferred by the lamps is real, so the loss is attributed to the current.
misconceptions.correction: What the lamps use is energy, not charge. Every coulomb that leaves the cell passes through both lamps and returns, so the current is identical everywhere in the loop.

misconceptions.question: How should an ammeter and a voltmeter be connected to a component?
misconceptions.correct: The ammeter goes in series with the component and the voltmeter in parallel with it.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltmeter goes in the loop with the component and the ammeter goes across it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both instruments look alike and both are 'meters', so students remember that one goes in series and one in parallel but not which. Nothing in the symbols themselves distinguishes them.
misconceptions.correction: Current passes through a component, so the ammeter must be in the same loop for the same current to pass through it. Potential difference is across a component, so the voltmeter must be connected across the same two points.

misconceptions.question: A cell is connected to a resistor, then to a resistor of higher resistance. Is the current the same both times?
misconceptions.correct: No. For a given potential difference, the greater the resistance the smaller the current.
misconceptions.misconception: A cell always pushes out the same current, so changing the component cannot change the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cells are labelled with a fixed value (1.5 V) and students read this as a fixed 'amount of electricity' the cell delivers, rather than as a potential difference.
misconceptions.correction: The label gives the potential difference, not the current. The current is set by both the pd and the resistance, through I = V ÷ R, so a larger resistance gives a smaller current.

misconceptions.question: A current of 0.20 A flows for 5.0 minutes. What is the charge flow?
misconceptions.correct: 60 C. The time must be converted to seconds: Q = 0.20 × 300 = 60 C.
misconceptions.misconception: You can put the time straight into Q = I t in whatever units the question gives, so the answer is 1.0 C.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation does not itself say 'seconds', and in everyday arithmetic units are rarely converted first. The number in the question feels like the number to use.
misconceptions.correction: In Q = I t, time t is in seconds, s. Convert minutes to seconds by multiplying by 60 before substituting, or the answer is out by a factor of 60.

misconceptions.question: What is electric current?
misconceptions.correct: Electric current is a flow of electrical charge, and its size is the rate of flow of electrical charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Current is the flow of energy round the circuit, or how fast the electrons are moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy transfer is the visible effect of a circuit, and 'flow' suggests speed. Both ideas are close enough to sound right in a sentence.
misconceptions.correction: Current counts how much charge passes a point each second, not how much energy is delivered and not how fast the charges travel. Charges drift very slowly even when the current is large.

misconceptions.question: Is a filament lamp an ohmic conductor?
misconceptions.correct: No. The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases, so its I-V graph is a curve.
misconceptions.misconception: A filament lamp is ohmic because its I-V graph goes through the origin and the current still rises when the pd rises.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'through the origin' as the test for proportionality and stop checking whether the line is straight. Any rising graph looks like proportionality.
misconceptions.correction: Direct proportionality needs a straight line through the origin. The lamp's graph passes through the origin but bends, becoming less steep, because the hot filament has a greater resistance.

misconceptions.question: A thermistor is warmed. What happens to its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases. The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating anything raises its resistance, so a hot thermistor has a higher resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The filament lamp is met first, and its resistance rises with temperature. Students generalise that rule to every component.
misconceptions.correction: A thermistor behaves in the opposite way to a metal wire: warming it lowers its resistance, which is exactly why it is useful as a temperature sensor.

misconceptions.question: Light on an LDR gets brighter. What happens to its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases. The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.
misconceptions.misconception: More light means more for the LDR to resist, so brighter light raises its resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name 'light-dependent resistor' tells students the resistance depends on light but not in which direction, and 'more light, more resistance' is the easier pattern to imagine.
misconceptions.correction: Bright light lowers an LDR's resistance and darkness raises it. Remember it through the application: in the dark the resistance is high, and that is what the control circuit uses to switch a lamp on.

misconceptions.question: What does a diode do when connected the reverse way round?
misconceptions.correct: Almost no current passes, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
misconceptions.misconception: A diode lets a smaller current through backwards, and has no resistance at all forwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'One direction only' is remembered as 'easier one way', which suggests a reduced rather than a blocked current, and the forward direction is then imagined as completely free.
misconceptions.correction: In the reverse direction the resistance is very high and the current through a diode flows in one direction only. In the forward direction the diode still has resistance, and it needs a large enough pd before it conducts well.

misconceptions.question: A wire is made twice as long at constant temperature. What happens to its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles. Resistance increases as the length of the wire increases.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer wire gives the charge more room to move, so the resistance is smaller.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture a wide pipe rather than a long one and confuse length with thickness, where more space really does mean an easier flow.
misconceptions.correction: Extra length means more wire for the charge to pass through, so more opposition. Length and resistance rise together; it is greater thickness, not greater length, that lowers resistance.

misconceptions.question: A second identical resistor is added in parallel. What happens to the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases, because the charge now has more than one path to flow along.
misconceptions.misconception: Two resistors must resist more than one, so adding any extra resistor raises the total resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule for series resistors - add them up - is learned first and applied to every combination without checking how the components are connected.
misconceptions.correction: Only in series do resistances add. In parallel each extra branch is another path for charge, so the total resistance falls below the resistance of the smallest single resistor.

misconceptions.question: Does every component have a fixed resistance?
misconceptions.correct: No. For some resistors the value of R remains constant, but in others it changes as the current changes.
misconceptions.misconception: Resistance is a fixed property of a component, like its mass, so it never changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resistors are sold with a single value printed on them, and V = I R is often practised only with a fixed number for R, so R looks like a constant of the component.
misconceptions.correction: R stays constant only for an ohmic conductor at a constant temperature. For lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs the resistance is not constant; it changes with the current through the component.

misconceptions.question: On an I-V graph, what does a steeper line tell you about the resistance?
misconceptions.correct: A steeper line means a smaller resistance, because resistance is V ÷ I, not I ÷ V.
misconceptions.misconception: The steeper the I-V graph, the greater the resistance, because resistance is the gradient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that gradient carries the physical meaning on a graph and take the gradient to be the resistance, without checking which quantity is on which axis.
misconceptions.correction: With current on the vertical axis and pd on the horizontal axis, the gradient is I ÷ V, which is 1 ÷ R. So a steep graph means a large current for a small pd - a low resistance.

misconceptions.question: Does potential difference flow through a component?
misconceptions.correct: No. Current flows through a component; potential difference is across it.
misconceptions.misconception: Potential difference flows through a component in the same way as current does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are introduced together as things a cell provides, and everyday speech says 'the voltage going through the wire'.
misconceptions.correction: Use the wiring to fix the idea: an ammeter goes in the loop because current passes through, while a voltmeter goes across two points because potential difference is the difference between them.

misconceptions.question: How is V = I R rearranged to find the resistance?
misconceptions.correct: R = V ÷ I. Divide the potential difference by the current.
misconceptions.misconception: To find R you multiply, so R = V × I, and to find I you work out R ÷ V.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is memorised as three letters with a multiplication sign, and under pressure students combine the two known numbers with whichever operation comes to mind.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Check the answer for sense: a 12 V supply driving 0.5 A must give a resistance of tens of ohms, not a few.

misconceptions.question: A room controlled by a thermostat cools down. What does the thermistor do?
misconceptions.correct: Its resistance rises as the temperature falls, and the control circuit responds by switching the heater on.
misconceptions.misconception: When the room gets cold the thermistor's resistance falls, letting more current through to switch the heater on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly link 'heater on' with 'more current' and then work backwards to a falling resistance, without checking the direction of the thermistor's temperature response.
misconceptions.correction: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases, so cooling raises it. It is the rise in the thermistor's resistance that the control circuit detects and uses to switch the heater on.

misconceptions.question: A street lamp is switched on by an LDR circuit. What does the LDR do as night falls?
misconceptions.correct: Its resistance rises as the light intensity falls, and the control circuit switches the lamp on.
misconceptions.misconception: As it gets dark the LDR's resistance falls, and that is what turns the street lamp on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Switching something on sounds like making it easier for current to flow, so students assume the sensor's resistance must drop at the moment the lamp lights.
misconceptions.correction: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases, so darkness raises it. The control circuit senses the high resistance in the dark and switches the lamp on.

misconceptions.question: Which component is drawn as a rectangle with a diagonal arrow across it?
misconceptions.correct: A variable resistor.
misconceptions.misconception: A rectangle with an arrow across it is a thermistor, or an LDR - anything whose resistance can change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Four symbols are built on the same rectangle, so students remember 'resistor with something added' and then guess which addition belongs to which component.
misconceptions.correction: The diagonal arrow means a resistance you change by hand: a variable resistor. A thermistor is the rectangle with a line bent at right angles across it; an LDR is a rectangle in a circle with two arrows pointing in at it.

misconceptions.question: Why is the switch closed only briefly for each reading in the wire-length practical?
misconceptions.correct: So that the wire does not heat up, keeping the investigation at constant temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: It only saves the battery - the wire's temperature makes no difference to the resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The wire never feels hot to the touch, so the heating seems irrelevant, and 'save the battery' is a familiar reason for switching things off.
misconceptions.correction: A current warms the wire, and a warmer metal wire has a greater resistance. The specification requires the length of a wire to be investigated at constant temperature, so the current is kept flowing for as short a time as possible.

misconceptions.question: How do you obtain the reverse characteristic of a diode in Required practical activity 4?
misconceptions.correct: Reverse the connections of the diode itself and repeat the readings.
misconceptions.misconception: You swap the ammeter and voltmeter round, and that gives you the reverse readings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reverse the circuit' is remembered without specifying what is reversed, and the meters are the parts students handle most, so they are the obvious things to move.
misconceptions.correction: It is the diode's own connections that must be turned round, so that the pd is applied across it in the opposite direction. The ammeter stays in series and the voltmeter stays across the diode.

misconceptions.question: A copper wire is joined into a complete loop. Does a current flow?
misconceptions.correct: No. The circuit must also include a source of potential difference for charge to flow.
misconceptions.misconception: A complete loop is enough on its own - the charges are already in the metal, so they will go round it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Complete circuit' is drilled as the condition for a current, and the cell is treated as just another component rather than as the thing that drives the charge.
misconceptions.correction: Both conditions are needed: the circuit must be closed and it must include a source of potential difference. Without a cell there is nothing to make the charges flow one way round the loop.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between charge flow and current?
misconceptions.correct: Charge flow is a quantity of charge, in coulombs, C; current is the rate of flow of charge, in amperes, A.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge and current are the same thing, so coulombs and amperes are two names for one unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are introduced in the same equation and both are described using the word 'charge', so the distinction between an amount and a rate is easily lost.
misconceptions.correction: Current tells you how much charge passes each second; charge flow tells you how much passed altogether. They are linked by Q = I t, so 2 A flowing for 3 s gives a charge flow of 6 C.

misconceptions.question: When measuring a wire's resistance, where should the voltmeter be connected?
misconceptions.correct: Across the test wire itself, so it measures the potential difference across that wire.
misconceptions.misconception: It does not matter, because the potential difference across the cell is the same as across the wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In simple circuits with one component the two readings are nearly equal, so students conclude that the voltmeter can go anywhere convenient.
misconceptions.correction: Resistance is found from the pd across the component divided by the current through it, so the voltmeter must be across that component. Other parts of the circuit, such as the ammeter and connecting leads, take a share of the cell's pd.

mcqs.stem: In a circuit diagram, one component is drawn as a rectangle with an arrow across it at an angle. Which component is it?

options.text: a variable resistor, whose resistance is changed by moving a slider
options.rationale: The standard symbol for a variable resistor is the resistor rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it, showing a resistance that can be set by hand.

options.text: a thermistor, whose resistance changes when its temperature changes
options.rationale: Students who know several symbols are built on the same rectangle guess the one whose resistance varies with temperature; the thermistor symbol has a line bent at right angles, not an arrow.

options.text: an LDR, whose resistance falls when the light on it gets brighter
options.rationale: Another 'changing resistance' component, so it attracts the same guess; the LDR symbol is a rectangle inside a circle with two arrows pointing in at it.

options.text: a diode, which allows a current through it in one direction only
options.rationale: The arrow tempts students who remember that the diode symbol contains an arrowhead, but the diode symbol is a triangle against a line, not a rectangle.

mcqs.stem: A student needs to measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?

options.text: the voltmeter in series with the lamp, the ammeter in parallel with it
options.rationale: A straight swap by a student who knows one meter goes in series and one in parallel but cannot recall which is which.

options.text: the ammeter in series with the lamp, the voltmeter in parallel with it
options.rationale: The same current must pass through the ammeter as through the lamp, so it goes in the loop; pd is measured between two points, so the voltmeter goes across the lamp.

options.text: both meters in parallel with the lamp, connected across the same points
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think potential difference flows through a component just as current does, so both meters must sit in the same place.

options.text: both meters in series with the lamp, one on each side of the lamp
options.rationale: Appeals to students who think every meter must have the circuit's current passing through it to give a reading.

mcqs.stem: A length of copper wire is joined into a complete loop with no cell in it. Which statement is correct?

options.text: charge flows, because the circuit is a complete and unbroken loop
options.rationale: Students drilled on 'a current needs a complete circuit' treat that condition as sufficient on its own.

options.text: charge flows, but only until the charge in the copper is used up
options.rationale: Combines the same error with the idea that charge is consumed, giving a current that starts and then dies away.

options.text: no charge flows, because there is no source of potential difference
options.rationale: For charge to flow the circuit must be closed and include a source of potential difference; this loop meets only the first condition.

options.text: no charge flows, because copper has too little resistance to it
options.rationale: Picked by students who think resistance is what drives a current rather than what opposes it.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about electric current is correct?

options.text: it is a flow of energy, and its size is the rate of flow of energy
options.rationale: Energy transfer is what students see happening in a lamp, so current is taken to be the energy on the move.

options.text: it is the amount of charge that has passed, measured in coulombs
options.rationale: Confuses current with charge flow: an amount rather than a rate, and the wrong unit with it.

options.text: it is the speed of the electrons, and its size is how fast they go
options.rationale: The word 'flow' suggests speed, and students picture fast-moving electrons rather than a rate of charge.

options.text: it is a flow of charge, and its size is the rate of flow of charge
options.rationale: This is the definition in the specification: current is a flow of electrical charge and its size is the rate of flow of electrical charge.

mcqs.stem: A current of 0.25 A flows through a lamp for 3.0 minutes. What is the charge flow through the lamp?

options.rationale: Q = I t with t in seconds: 3.0 minutes is 180 s, so Q = 0.25 × 180 = 45 C.
The time is left in minutes: 0.25 × 3.0 = 0.75, an answer 60 times too small.
The equation is rearranged wrongly and the numbers divided: 180 ÷ 0.25 = 720.
The converted time is written down as the answer, with the multiplication by the current forgotten.

mcqs.stem: Which units must be used in the equation charge flow = current × time?

options.text: charge flow in coulombs, C; current in amperes, A; time in minutes, min
options.rationale: Chosen by students who never convert times, so minutes look like an acceptable unit in the equation.

options.text: charge flow in coulombs, C; current in amperes, A; time in seconds, s
options.rationale: These are the units the specification gives for Q, I and t in Q = I t.

options.text: charge flow in amperes, A; current in coulombs, C; time in seconds, s
options.rationale: The two electrical units are swapped by students who do not separate an amount of charge from a rate of flow.

options.text: charge flow in coulombs, C; current in volts, V; time in seconds, s
options.rationale: Volts are attached to the current by students who blur potential difference and current together.

mcqs.stem: Two lamps are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the first lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the two lamps. What does it read?

options.text: less than 0.30 A, because the first lamp uses up some of the current
options.rationale: The commonest error in series circuits: the lamp is seen to consume the current rather than energy.

options.text: 0.15 A, because the current is shared equally between the two lamps
options.rationale: A more specific version of the same idea, borrowing the sharing rule that belongs to parallel branches.

options.text: 0.30 A, because the current is the same at any point in the loop
options.rationale: There is one closed loop, and a current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.

options.text: 0.30 A, but only while the two lamps have equal resistance values
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds cautious, but the equality of current does not depend on the components being identical.

mcqs.stem: Component X and component Y are each connected in turn across the same 6 V supply. X has a greater resistance than Y. Which statement is correct?

options.text: the current through X is greater than the current through Y
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship, treating a large resistance as something that gives a large current.

options.text: the current through X is the same as the current through Y
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the supply fixes the current whatever is connected to it.

options.text: the pd across X is smaller than the pd across Y
options.rationale: Ignores the stem: both are connected across the same 6 V supply, so the pd is the same for each.

options.text: the current through X is smaller than the current through Y
options.rationale: For a given potential difference, the greater the resistance the smaller the current.

mcqs.stem: The potential difference across a resistor is 6.0 V and the current through it is 0.40 A. What is its resistance?

options.rationale: The known values are multiplied: 6.0 × 0.40 = 2.4.
The division is done the wrong way round: 0.40 ÷ 6.0 = 0.067.
Only the current is used, as 1 ÷ 0.40, with the potential difference left out.

mcqs.stem: A 48 Ω resistor is connected across a 12 V supply. What is the current through the resistor?

options.rationale: The division is inverted: 48 ÷ 12 = 4.0.
The equation is used unrearranged and the values multiplied: 12 × 48 = 576.
Halving 12 and then dividing by 48 gives 0.25, but students who halve at the end instead reach 0.50.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student measures the resistance of 20 cm of nichrome wire, then of 40 cm of the same wire at the same temperature. The resistance of the 40 cm length is:

options.text: about half as large, because a longer wire gives the charge more room
options.rationale: Length is confused with thickness, where more space really does make the flow easier.

options.text: the same, because it is the same wire at the same temperature
options.rationale: Treats resistance as a fixed property of the material, forgetting that length is the variable being changed.

options.text: about twice as large, because resistance increases with the length
options.rationale: At constant temperature the resistance of a wire increases with its length, so doubling the length doubles the resistance.

options.text: about twice as large, but only because the longer wire gets hotter
options.rationale: Gets the numerical answer right for the wrong reason; the investigation is done at constant temperature.

mcqs.stem: A student adds a second identical resistor in parallel with the first. What happens to the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it increases, because two resistors must resist more than one alone
options.rationale: The everyday idea that adding more of something always adds more opposition.

options.text: it doubles, because the two resistance values are added together
options.rationale: Applies the series rule to a parallel combination, which is the most frequent version of this error.

options.text: it stays the same, because each resistor keeps its own value
options.rationale: Confuses the unchanged value of each individual resistor with the resistance of the combination.

options.text: it decreases, because there is now more than one path for the charge
options.rationale: Each parallel branch is an extra route for charge, so the total resistance falls below that of either resistor alone.

mcqs.stem: In the wire-length investigation the switch is closed only briefly while each pair of readings is taken. Why?

options.text: to stop the wire heating up, so the temperature is kept constant
options.rationale: A current warms the wire and a warmer wire has a greater resistance, so brief readings keep the investigation at constant temperature.

options.text: to save the cell, since the temperature of the wire has no effect
options.rationale: A familiar everyday reason for switching off, chosen by students who think the warming is irrelevant.

options.text: because the resistance of a wire is fixed, so one reading will do
options.rationale: Treats resistance as an unchanging property, so repeated readings seem pointless.

options.text: to stop the large current in the shortest wire damaging the meter
options.rationale: Plausible laboratory caution, but the reason the specification gives is the constant temperature of the wire.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of measurements lets a student calculate the resistance of each length of test wire?

options.text: the potential difference across the cell and the current through the wire
options.rationale: Students assume the cell's pd equals the pd across the wire, so the voltmeter can be connected anywhere.

options.text: the potential difference across the test wire and the current through it
options.rationale: Resistance is found from R = V ÷ I, using the pd across the wire and the current through that same wire.

options.text: the current through the test wire and the charge that flows in one minute
options.rationale: Reaches for Q = I t because charge and current are the electrical quantities most recently met.

options.text: the potential difference across the wire and the length of the wire used
options.rationale: Length is the independent variable of the investigation, not a quantity that appears in R = V ÷ I.

mcqs.stem: Which component has a resistance that stays constant as the current through it changes?

options.text: a filament lamp, once it has fully warmed up
options.rationale: Students assume a lamp settles to one resistance, but its resistance rises further as the current rises.

options.text: a thermistor in a room at a steady temperature
options.rationale: Sounds like the constant-temperature condition, but the specification lists thermistors as components whose resistance is not constant.

options.text: a fixed resistor held at a constant temperature
options.rationale: An ohmic conductor at a constant temperature has a resistance that remains constant as the current changes.

options.text: a diode connected the right way round in a loop
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a forward-connected diode behaves like an ordinary resistor.

mcqs.stem: The I-V graph of a component at constant temperature is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?

options.text: the resistance of the component rises steadily as the pd across it rises
options.rationale: Students see the rising line and read the rise as an increase in resistance rather than in current.

options.text: the resistance is equal to the gradient of the line at every point on it
options.rationale: Gradient is assumed to be the resistance; with I on the vertical axis the gradient is in fact 1 ÷ R.

options.text: the component must be a filament lamp, whose graph goes through the origin
options.rationale: The lamp's graph does pass through the origin, so students who ignore straightness pick it.

options.text: the current is directly proportional to the pd, so the resistance is constant
options.rationale: A straight line through the origin is the graphical test for direct proportionality, and it means R stays the same as the current changes.

mcqs.stem: The potential difference across a filament lamp is increased from 2 V to 12 V. What happens to the resistance of the filament?

options.text: it is greater at 12 V, because the filament is hotter
options.rationale: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases, and the larger current heats it more.

options.text: it is smaller at 12 V, because the filament is hotter
options.rationale: Applies the thermistor's behaviour to a metal filament, so hotter is read as less resistive.

options.text: it is the same at 12 V, because the lamp is an ohmic conductor
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat every component as ohmic once the temperature is not mentioned.

options.text: it is smaller at 12 V, because more current means less resistance
options.rationale: Uses a remembered inverse rule between current and resistance without reference to the filament's temperature.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a diode is correct?

options.text: it has a small resistance in the reverse direction, so a small current flows back
options.rationale: 'One direction only' is softened into 'easier one way', giving a reduced rather than a blocked current.

options.text: it has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so current flows one way
options.rationale: The current through a diode flows in one direction only, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

options.text: it has zero resistance in the forward direction, whatever the pd across it
options.rationale: The forward direction is imagined as completely free, ignoring the pd needed before the diode conducts.

options.text: it has an equal resistance in both directions until the pd is large enough
options.rationale: Treats resistance as one fixed property of the component that a threshold pd then switches on.

mcqs.stem: A thermistor is connected to a fixed potential difference and is then warmed from 20 °C to 60 °C. What happens?

options.text: its resistance increases, so the current through it decreases
options.rationale: The filament lamp's temperature behaviour is generalised to the thermistor.

options.text: its resistance increases, so the current through it stays the same
options.rationale: Combines the wrong temperature response with the belief that the supply fixes the current.

options.text: its resistance decreases, so the current through it increases
options.rationale: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases, and at a fixed pd a smaller resistance gives a larger current.

options.text: its resistance decreases, so the current through it also decreases
options.rationale: Gets the resistance right but links resistance and current the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: A thermistor is used in the control circuit of a thermostat for a room heater. The room cools down. What happens?

options.text: the thermistor's resistance falls, and the larger current switches it on
options.rationale: Students reason backwards from 'heater on means more current' to a falling resistance.

options.text: the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit switches the heater off
options.rationale: Gets the resistance change right but then applies it in the wrong direction to the heater.

options.text: the thermistor's resistance falls, so the heater stays off until it warms
options.rationale: Combines the wrong temperature response with the wrong switching outcome.

options.text: the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit switches the heater on
options.rationale: Cooling raises a thermistor's resistance, and the control circuit uses that change to switch the heater on.

mcqs.stem: The light falling on an LDR becomes brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?

options.text: it decreases, because an LDR's resistance falls as light intensity rises
options.rationale: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.

options.text: it increases, because brighter light meets more resistance in the LDR
options.rationale: 'More light, more resistance' is the easier pattern to picture from the component's name.

options.text: it increases, in the same way as a filament lamp's resistance rises
options.rationale: Borrows the filament lamp's rising resistance as a general rule for all components.

options.text: it stays the same, because only its temperature affects an LDR
options.rationale: Confuses the LDR with the thermistor, the other sensing component in the same list.

mcqs.stem: An LDR is used in a circuit that switches a street lamp on when it gets dark. What happens as night falls?

options.text: the LDR's resistance falls, and the larger current switches the lamp on
options.rationale: Switching on is assumed to require an easier path for current, so the resistance is thought to drop.

options.text: the LDR's resistance rises, and the circuit switches the street lamp on
options.rationale: Falling light intensity raises the LDR's resistance, and the control circuit uses that change to switch the lamp on.

options.text: the LDR's resistance rises, and this switches the street lamp off till dawn
options.rationale: Gets the resistance change right but reverses what the circuit does with it.

options.text: the LDR's resistance stays the same, and a timer switches the lamp on
options.rationale: A real alternative technology, chosen by students unsure that the LDR itself responds to darkness.

mcqs.stem: A circuit is built to measure the resistance of a component, using a cell, a switch, an ammeter, a voltmeter and a variable resistor. What is the variable resistor for?

options.text: to measure the current, so that the ammeter is not needed in the loop
options.rationale: Confuses a component that controls the current with one of the meters that reads it.

options.text: to keep the resistance of the component constant while it is measured
options.rationale: Assumes resistance must be held fixed rather than measured at several different currents.

options.text: to change the current, so that several pairs of readings can be taken
options.rationale: Adjusting the variable resistor alters the current through the component, giving a set of current and pd pairs from which resistance can be found.

options.text: to protect the voltmeter from the full potential difference of the cell
options.rationale: Sounds like sensible protection, but a voltmeter is designed to be connected across the supply pd.

mcqs.stem: An I-V graph for a circuit element is a curve that becomes less steep as the current increases. What does the graph show?

options.text: the element is non-linear, and its resistance decreases as the current rises
options.rationale: Reads the falling gradient as a falling resistance, forgetting that with I on the vertical axis the gradient is 1 ÷ R.

options.text: the element is linear, because the curve still passes through the origin
options.rationale: Uses 'through the origin' as the whole test and ignores whether the graph is straight.

options.text: the element is non-linear, but its resistance is the same at every current
options.rationale: Accepts the curve but keeps hold of the idea that a component has one fixed resistance.

options.text: the element is non-linear, and its resistance increases as the current rises
options.rationale: A curve means the element is non-linear; a graph becoming less steep means a smaller current for each extra volt, so the resistance is rising.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 4, how does a student obtain the reverse characteristic of a diode?

options.text: by reversing the connections of the diode and repeating the readings
options.rationale: Turning the diode round applies the pd across it in the opposite direction, so the reverse part of the I-V characteristic can be measured.

options.text: by swapping the ammeter and the voltmeter and repeating the readings
options.rationale: 'Reverse the circuit' is remembered without specifying what is reversed, and the meters are the obvious parts to move.

options.text: by connecting the ammeter across the diode instead of in series with it
options.rationale: Another meter-moving answer, from students unsure which meter belongs in which position.

options.text: by turning the pd down to zero, since a diode conducts in both directions
options.rationale: Assumes the diode passes some current in reverse, so no change of connections seems necessary.
